To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) end-to-end learning methods can outperform hand-designed feature engineering methods, (2) end-to-end learned methods can be used in a transfer learning context, and (3) transfer learning methods can out-perform methods trained on the same data set.

1) SASNet, the first end-to end deep learning method for protein binding site prediction, outperforms state of the art methods, 2) SASNet is the first method to use only atomic coordinates and atom identities as inputs and 3) our results demonstrate the first successful application transfer learning to atomic level data.

we have demonstrated the first successful application, to date, of transfer learning to atomically detailed protein structures and that we have developed the first end-to- end learning method for protein binding site prediction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of protein-protein interactions and the question of how to learn representations of protein structures that can be applied to other problems.
the question of how to represent atomic structures in a learning framework.
the question of how to best represent protein structure data in a machine learning framework.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we present the first end-to end learning method for protein binding site prediction, and that it outperforms state of the art methods.

our work presents a novel approach to the problem of protein interface prediction, and that our method is able to learn representations of protein structures that outperform existing methods, and that are transferable to new data sets.
SASNet is an end-to-end learning approach for protein interface prediction that uses only atomic-level data as input, and outperforms state of the art methods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a novel deep learning method for protein-protein interface prediction that outperforms state of the art methods and is the first to be able to transfer from one protein to another.
we present a new, end-to-end, deep learning approach that can be used to predict how proteins interact with other proteins.
we present the first deep learning model that learns a generalizable representation of protein surfaces, which we show to be transferable across different protein interfaces.
The main takeaway from our work is that
end-to-end learning methods can outperform hand-crafted features and are highly transferrable, even when the underlying physics is not well understood.
, with sufficient training data, end-to-end learning is a powerful tool for protein structure prediction.
the raw spatial coordinates of atoms can be leveraged to learn representations of protein surfaces that are more generalizable than hand-designed features.
